apis_http.notes: HTTP/API concepts only; the requests library is lib_requests and urllib is lib_urllib. Worked examples with live endpoints use canned JSON (as Python data) and say what the live call returns. Rate limits (429) are lib_requests.handle_errors and automation.reliable_bots. Building your own API (REST design, Flask routes) is B17 rest_api_design, which should list apis_http.request_response_cycle (methods, status codes) as a prerequisite. OAuth flows (Spotipy) and SMS (Twilio) were not given topics: library-specific and project-shaped. LLM APIs (B20) can depend on lib_requests.send_data_and_headers. Every B16 topic is non-core: none run in a browser sandbox without network access.

lib_requests.notes: Snippets were checked offline with requests 2.31 under the system Python 3.9 (requests.Request(...).prepare() for URLs and bodies, hand-built Response objects for .json() and raise_for_status); no live calls. Sessions, file uploads and streaming downloads were left out.

lib_urllib.notes: urllib.request (py4e's urlopen) plus urllib.parse; urllib.robotparser is used in web_scraping.scrape_responsibly. urlopen behaviour was checked offline with data: URLs.

web_scraping.notes: html_css_basics is out of scope (plan.json), so html_and_regex KP1 teaches just enough HTML (tags, attributes, nesting, class/id) to scrape. follow_links stands in a dict of link lists for fetch+parse so the crawl logic is testable; it encompasses graph_algorithms.breadth_first_search as non_ancestor. Ethics of scraping (100 Days Day 45) is scrape_responsibly. Teaching order: html_and_regex, scrape_responsibly, then lib_beautifulsoup topics, then scrape_to_records and follow_links.

lib_beautifulsoup.notes: bs4 is not installed here, so these snippets were NOT run; outputs follow documented Beautiful Soup 4 behaviour (find returns None, get vs [] on attributes, get_text(strip=True), select/select_one). Navigating siblings/parents and lxml as a parser were left out.

lib_selenium.notes: Not installed and needs a browser, so snippets were not run; written against the Selenium 4 API (By locators, find_element/find_elements; the old find_element_by_* methods are gone). Login automation for real social sites (100 Days Days 49-52) is project-shaped and was not given topics; the form-filling KP uses a generic form.

xml_parsing.notes: xml_documents (format) comes before the lib_elementtree topics; read_rss_feed (Boot.dev's RSS aggregator, py4e XML) comes after them. Using defusedxml for untrusted XML and XML Schema (py4e lecture) were not given KPs. Writing XML was left out.

lib_elementtree.notes: Uses 'import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET' (B13 from_import_and_alias covers the alias form). Creating and writing XML (SubElement, ET.tostring) was left out: no course teaches it.

web_services.notes: One non-core topic (py4e lecture, introduced). Includes the fetch/parse split so parsers can be tested with canned text. SOAP/WSDL were not taught.

networking_sockets.notes: One conceptual topic placed before apis_http, as the concept graph says. DNS, TLS and HTTP servers are out of scope per plan.json; TLS appears only as starttls in lib_smtplib.

lib_socket.notes: py4e's socket browser. send/recv behaviour was checked locally with socket.socketpair() (no network). Writing a socket server was left out (http_servers is out of scope).

tool_geocoding_api.notes: Uses py4e's current OpenGeo endpoint and its GeoJSON reply shape (features[0].properties.lat/lon/formatted); replies are canned. py4e's geoload.py caches in SQLite; here the cache is a dict/JSON file because sqlite3 is B17 (sibling). B17 lib_sqlite3 could add a practice item that swaps the cache for a table. Drawing the map itself is B18 data_visualization.

lib_smtplib.notes: smtplib calls need a real server and credentials, so only message building (string format, EmailMessage, encode errors) was run. Contact-form email from Flask (100 Days Day 60) belongs to B17 lib_flask and can depend on email_messages_and_templates. Attachments and HTML email were left out.

automation.notes: Problem-based topics built on the 100 Days birthday wisher, price tracker and rain alert. Concrete tools are owned by lib_smtplib, lib_selenium, lib_pyautogui and scheduling_cron. Logging uses plain file appends; the logging module has no concept in the plan. time.sleep is used as a memorised 'import time' line (B13 has no time-module concept). Bots that log in to real social sites were not given topics.

lib_pyautogui.notes: One non-core topic (100 Days Day 94, introduced). Not installed and needs a desktop, so snippets were not run. Screenshot-based image location (locateOnScreen) was left out.

scheduling_cron.notes: 100 Days Day 32 (PythonAnywhere). The third-party 'schedule' package and GitHub Actions cron were not given topics. B17 deployment can build on cron_and_cloud_schedulers.

topics.title: How programs talk over a network: hosts, ports and protocols
topics.summary: Describe a network conversation as a client connecting to a server's host and port and following a protocol, and look up a host's address with socket.gethostbyname.

knowledge_points.title: Clients ask, servers answer
knowledge_points.worked_example:
browser (client)  --request-->  web server
browser (client)  <--response--  web server
The client always speaks first; the server waits for connections.
knowledge_points.practice: For described situations (checking weather in an app, a website sending a page), name the client and the server and order the messages.

knowledge_points.title: Host names, IP addresses and DNS
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import socket
print(socket.gethostbyname("localhost"))  # 127.0.0.1
DNS turns a name into an address; for a real name such as "data.pr4e.org" the call asks a DNS server and returns its public IP.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result for localhost; choose which step (DNS lookup, connect, send) happens first.

knowledge_points.title: Ports pick the program on the host
knowledge_points.worked_example:
A host runs many servers; the port number picks one.
80 = HTTP, 443 = HTTPS, 587 = sending email (SMTP)
An address plus a port, e.g. ("data.pr4e.org", 80), names one endpoint.
knowledge_points.practice: Match services to their usual ports; write the (host, port) pair for a described server.

knowledge_points.title: Protocols are agreed rules, stacked in layers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
HTTP: what to say (GET /page, 200 OK)
TCP: deliver bytes reliably and in order, split into packets
IP: route each packet to the right address
Your program only speaks the top layer; the lower ones are handled for it.
knowledge_points.practice: Assign jobs to layers; predict what a program sees when packets arrive out of order (TCP reorders them).

topics.title: The HTTP request-response cycle
topics.summary: Read a URL's parts, the text of an HTTP request and response, status codes and the four main methods.

knowledge_points.title: The parts of a URL
knowledge_points.worked_example:
url = "https://api.example.com/v1/weather?city=Oslo&units=metric"
address, query = url.split("?")
print(query)  # city=Oslo&units=metric
scheme https, host api.example.com, path /v1/weather, query after the ?
knowledge_points.practice: Label the scheme, host, path and query of given URLs; predict what a split on ? or & gives.

knowledge_points.title: What a request and a response look like
knowledge_points.worked_example:
GET /romeo.txt HTTP/1.0
Host: data.pr4e.org
(blank line)
---
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain
(blank line)
But soft what light ...
First line, headers, a blank line, then the body.
knowledge_points.practice: Label the request line, status line, headers and body of raw HTTP text; order scrambled request lines.

knowledge_points.title: Status codes tell you what happened
knowledge_points.worked_example:
200 OK, 201 Created: success (2xx)
301 Moved Permanently: go elsewhere (3xx)
401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests: your request's fault (4xx)
500 Internal Server Error: the server's fault (5xx)
knowledge_points.practice: Classify codes by family; for each scenario (wrong API key, typo in path, server crash) pick the likely code.

knowledge_points.title: Methods: GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, DELETE
knowledge_points.worked_example:
GET /habits          read the list
POST /habits         create a habit (data in the body)
PUT /habits/7        replace habit 7; PATCH changes part of it
DELETE /habits/7     remove it
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the method for described actions; spot a request that uses GET to change data.

topics.title: Reading API documentation: endpoints, parameters and keys
topics.summary: Turn an API's documentation into a working request: endpoint, required and optional parameters, the API key, and the shape of the JSON it returns.

knowledge_points.title: Endpoint plus parameters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Docs: GET https://api.sunrise-sunset.org/json  params: lat (required), lng (required), formatted (optional, 0 or 1)
Request: https://api.sunrise-sunset.org/json?lat=51.5&lng=-0.12&formatted=0
knowledge_points.practice: Write the full URL for a documented request; find the missing required parameter in a broken one.

knowledge_points.title: Use the documented response shape
knowledge_points.practice: Given a documented JSON example, write the expression that reaches a named field.

knowledge_points.title: API keys: who you are, kept out of the code
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Docs: pass appid=<your key> as a parameter (some APIs use a header instead)
import os
key = os.environ.get("OWM_API_KEY")
A 401 response usually means the key is missing or wrong.
knowledge_points.practice: Find where the docs put the key; fix code that hard-codes it; diagnose a 401.

knowledge_points.title: Text that arrives HTML-escaped
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import html
q = "Which planet is the "Red Planet"?"
print(html.unescape(q))  # Which planet is the "Red Planet"?
Some APIs (Open Trivia DB) escape quotes and & in their text.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict unescaped strings; add the missing unescape step to a quiz program.

topics.title: Turning API responses into answers
topics.summary: Process parsed JSON responses (given here as Python data, as the live calls would return) into the values a program needs, including feeding one API's result into the next.

knowledge_points.title: Pull out values and convert them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = {"message": "success", "iss_position": {"latitude": "-12.3456", "longitude": "101.2345"}}
lat = float(data["iss_position"]["latitude"])
print(lat)  # -12.3456
This is what api.open-notify.org/iss-now.json returns; numbers often arrive as strings.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict extracted values; fix code that compares a string coordinate with a number.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over a list in the response
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the flag for given forecasts; write the loop that counts or finds matching items.

knowledge_points.title: Reshape results for your program
knowledge_points.worked_example:
questions = []
for r in response["results"]:
    questions.append((html.unescape(r["question"]), r["correct_answer"] == "True"))
print(questions[0])  # ('The "Red Planet" is Mars.', True)
knowledge_points.practice: Build a list of tuples or dicts from a response; predict its first item.

knowledge_points.title: Chain two APIs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
days = list(daily["Time Series (Daily)"].values())
latest = float(days[0]["4. close"])
before = float(days[1]["4. close"])
change = (latest - before) / before * 100
print(round(change, 1))  # 5.0
if abs(change) >= 5: fetch news for the stock from a second API
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps of a two-API program; predict whether the second call happens for given prices.

topics.title: Fetching data with requests
topics.summary: Install requests, make a GET request, check the status code, read .text or .json(), pass parameters with params= and always set a timeout.

knowledge_points.title: A first GET request
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import requests   # python3 -m pip install requests
response = requests.get("https://api.kanye.rest", timeout=10)
print(response.status_code)  # 200
print(response.json()["quote"])  # e.g. a random quote
knowledge_points.practice: Order the lines of a GET program; predict which line prints the status code.

knowledge_points.title: .text is a string, .json() is Python data
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type(response.text))    # <class 'str'>
print(type(response.json()))  # <class 'dict'>
.json() does json.loads(response.text) for you.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict types and values from .text and .json() for a given response body; fix code that indexes .text like a dict.

knowledge_points.title: Parameters with params=
knowledge_points.worked_example:
params = {"lat": 51.5, "lng": -0.12, "formatted": 0}
r = requests.get("https://api.sunrise-sunset.org/json", params=params, timeout=10)
print(r.url)  # https://api.sunrise-sunset.org/json?lat=51.5&lng=-0.12&formatted=0
requests builds and encodes the query string.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the params dict for a documented request; predict the final URL.

knowledge_points.title: Always pass a timeout
knowledge_points.worked_example:
requests.get(url)               # may wait forever on a dead server
requests.get(url, timeout=10)   # gives up after 10 s with requests.exceptions.Timeout
knowledge_points.practice: Spot the calls without a timeout; choose sensible timeouts for described programs.

topics.title: Sending data with requests: POST, PUT, DELETE and headers
topics.summary: Create, update and delete resources on an API by sending a JSON body and authentication headers.

knowledge_points.title: POST a JSON body
knowledge_points.practice: Write a POST that sends a given dict; predict which method the docs require for creating an item.

knowledge_points.title: Authenticate with headers
knowledge_points.practice: Write the headers dict for documented auth schemes; fix a request that puts the token in the wrong place.

knowledge_points.title: PUT and DELETE address one item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pixel_url = graph_url + "/20241012"
requests.put(pixel_url, json={"quantity": "7.5"}, headers=headers, timeout=10)
requests.delete(pixel_url, headers=headers, timeout=10)
The item's id goes in the URL path.
knowledge_points.practice: Build the URL for a given item; choose put, post or delete for described changes.

knowledge_points.title: json= versus data=
knowledge_points.worked_example:
requests.post(url, json={"unit": "km"})  # body {"unit": "km"}, Content-Type application/json
requests.post(url, data={"unit": "km"})  # body unit=km, a web form
Use the one the API documents.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the body sent for json= and data=; fix a request rejected because it sent a form instead of JSON.

topics.title: When requests fail: status checks and exceptions
topics.summary: Detect failed requests with status codes and raise_for_status, catch network errors with RequestException, and cope with a body that is not JSON.

knowledge_points.title: A 404 is not an exception
knowledge_points.worked_example:
r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/x", timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, r.ok)  # 404 False
requests returns normally for 4xx and 5xx; your code must check.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict status_code and ok for described responses; add the missing check before .json().

knowledge_points.title: raise_for_status turns bad codes into errors
knowledge_points.worked_example:
r.raise_for_status()
# requests.exceptions.HTTPError: 404 Client Error: Not Found for url: https://api.example.com/x
Does nothing for 2xx codes.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which responses raise; place raise_for_status in a program.

knowledge_points.title: Catch the whole family with RequestException
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which except clause catches each failure; write a fetch function that returns None on failure.

knowledge_points.title: A body that is not JSON
knowledge_points.worked_example:
r.text  # '<html>oops</html>'
r.json()
# requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)
Error pages are often HTML; check the status before decoding.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which responses can be decoded; fix code that calls .json() on an error page.

topics.title: Reading a web page with urllib
topics.summary: Open a URL with the standard library's urllib.request, read it line by line or all at once, decode the bytes, and process the text.

knowledge_points.title: Open a URL and loop over its lines
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import urllib.request
fhand = urllib.request.urlopen("http://data.pr4e.org/romeo.txt")
for line in fhand:
    print(line.decode().strip())
Prints the 4 lines of romeo.txt, starting "But soft what light through yonder window breaks".
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for a page with given text; fix a loop that prints b'...' lines.

knowledge_points.title: read() gets everything as bytes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = urllib.request.urlopen(url).read()
print(type(data))  # <class 'bytes'>
text = data.decode()
Only the body arrives: urllib has already removed the headers.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict types and lengths; choose decode() or not for each step.

knowledge_points.title: Count words on a web page
knowledge_points.practice: Write the counting loop; predict counts for a page with given text.

knowledge_points.title: Bad URLs raise errors
knowledge_points.worked_example:
urllib.request.urlopen("http://data.pr4e.org/nothere.txt")
# urllib.error.HTTPError: HTTP Error 404: Not Found
Unlike requests, urllib raises for 4xx and 5xx codes.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls raise and which return; compare with what requests does.

topics.title: Downloading images and other binary files
topics.summary: Download a non-text file with urllib, check its type, save it with mode 'wb', and read large files in chunks.

knowledge_points.title: Save the bytes with mode 'wb'
knowledge_points.worked_example:
img = urllib.request.urlopen("http://data.pr4e.org/cover3.jpg").read()
with open("cover3.jpg", "wb") as fhand:
    fhand.write(img)
print(len(img))  # the size in bytes
knowledge_points.practice: Order the lines of a download; fix code that opens the output file in 'w' mode.

knowledge_points.title: Never decode binary data
knowledge_points.worked_example:
raw = b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"
raw.decode()
# UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x89 in position 0: invalid start byte
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which downloads can be decoded as text; remove the wrong decode() from a program.

knowledge_points.title: Check what you got: Content-Type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
page = urllib.request.urlopen(url)
print(page.headers["Content-Type"])  # e.g. image/jpeg
An error page would say text/html instead.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose text or binary handling from a Content-Type; predict the file extension to use.

knowledge_points.title: Read big files in chunks
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("cover3.jpg", "wb") as fhand:
    while True:
        chunk = img_page.read(100000)
        if len(chunk) < 1:
            break
        fhand.write(chunk)
read(n) returns b'' when the download is finished.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace chunk sizes for a file of given size; fill in the stop condition.

topics.title: Building URLs safely with urllib.parse
topics.summary: Split URLs into parts, build query strings with urlencode and quote, and turn relative links into absolute ones with urljoin.

knowledge_points.title: Split a URL with urlsplit
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit
parts = urlsplit("https://api.example.com/v1/weather?city=Oslo")
print(parts.netloc, parts.path)  # api.example.com /v1/weather
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the scheme, netloc, path and query of given URLs.

knowledge_points.title: Build a query string with urlencode
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from urllib.parse import urlencode
print(urlencode({"q": "fish & chips", "page": 2}))
# q=fish+%26+chips&page=2
Pasting "fish & chips" into a URL by hand would split it at the &.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict encoded query strings; fix a hand-built URL that breaks on spaces or &.

knowledge_points.title: Encode one piece with quote
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from urllib.parse import quote
print(quote("Ann Arbor, MI"))  # Ann%20Arbor%2C%20MI
Use it for a value that goes in the path rather than the query.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose quote or urlencode for described URLs; predict quoted text.

knowledge_points.title: Resolve relative links with urljoin
knowledge_points.worked_example:
base = "https://books.example.com/catalog/page1.html"
print(urljoin(base, "page2.html"))     # https://books.example.com/catalog/page2.html
print(urljoin(base, "/about.html"))    # https://books.example.com/about.html
print(urljoin(base, "../index.html"))  # https://books.example.com/index.html
knowledge_points.practice: Predict absolute URLs for relative links; fix a scraper that glues strings together with +.

topics.title: The world's simplest web browser with socket
topics.summary: Open a TCP connection with socket, send an HTTP GET request as bytes, receive the response in a loop until the server closes, and decode it.

knowledge_points.title: Connect to a host and port
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import socket
mysock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
mysock.connect(("data.pr4e.org", 80))
AF_INET + SOCK_STREAM means an internet TCP connection; connect takes one (host, port) tuple.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the connect call for a described server; fix a call that passes host and port as two arguments.

knowledge_points.title: Send the request as bytes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cmd = "GET http://data.pr4e.org/romeo.txt HTTP/1.0

".encode()
mysock.send(cmd)
mysock.send("GET / HTTP/1.0

")
# TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'
knowledge_points.practice: Write the request line for a given URL; fix sends that use str or forget the blank line.

knowledge_points.title: Receive until the server closes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
while True:
    data = mysock.recv(512)
    if len(data) < 1:
        break
    print(data.decode(), end="")
mysock.close()
recv returns at most 512 bytes; b'' means the server is done.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace how many recv calls a response of given length needs; fill in the stop condition.

knowledge_points.title: Collect the pieces before decoding
knowledge_points.worked_example:
chunks = []
while True:
    data = mysock.recv(512)
    if len(data) < 1:
        break
    chunks.append(data)
response = b"".join(chunks).decode()
A multi-byte character can be split across two chunks, so join first, decode once.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the safe order (join then decode); predict the joined response from given chunks.

topics.title: Taking apart a raw HTTP response
topics.summary: Split raw response bytes into status line, headers and body, read the status code and a header, and save a binary body to a file.

knowledge_points.title: Headers and body are split by a blank line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
raw = b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain

But soft what light"
head, body = raw.split(b"

", 1)
print(body.decode())  # But soft what light
knowledge_points.practice: Predict head and body for given raw responses; fix a split that uses "\n\n".

knowledge_points.title: Read the status code
knowledge_points.worked_example:
lines = head.decode().split("\r\n")
print(lines[0])             # HTTP/1.1 200 OK
print(lines[0].split()[1])  # 200
knowledge_points.practice: Extract the status code from status lines; decide whether to continue processing.

knowledge_points.title: Headers into a dictionary
knowledge_points.practice: Write the header loop; predict a header lookup.

knowledge_points.title: Save a binary body
knowledge_points.worked_example:
head, body = picture.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)
with open("stuff.jpg", "wb") as f:
    f.write(body)
Writing the headers into the file too would give a broken image.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that save headers with the image or decode the body.

topics.title: Reading HTML and pulling out links with regular expressions
topics.summary: Read the structure of an HTML page (tags, attributes, nesting, class and id) and extract simple data with re.findall, seeing why regex breaks on real HTML.

knowledge_points.title: Tags, attributes and nesting
knowledge_points.worked_example:
1) The Godfather

More
An element has a tag (div), attributes (class, id, href) and content; h3 and a are inside the div.
knowledge_points.practice: Name the tag, attributes and parent of marked elements in a snippet of HTML.

knowledge_points.title: Extract links with findall
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import re html = '

See Python and docs.

' print(re.findall(r'href="(.+?)"', html)) # ['https://python.org', '/docs']
knowledge_points.practice: Predict findall results on small pages; write a pattern for another attribute.

knowledge_points.title: The greedy-match bug
knowledge_points.worked_example: html = 'A B' print(re.findall(r'href="(.+)"', html)) # ['/a">A
knowledge_points.practice: Fix greedy patterns; predict output with and without ?.

knowledge_points.title: Why real pages need a parser
knowledge_points.worked_example: html = "Home FAQ" print(re.findall(r'href="(.+?)"', html)) # ['/faq'] Single quotes, extra attributes and line breaks are all legal HTML; an HTML parser handles them.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which legal HTML variants a pattern misses; choose regex or a parser for described jobs.

topics.title: Scraping responsibly: APIs first, robots.txt and polite requests
topics.summary: Decide whether to scrape at all, check robots.txt with urllib.robotparser, identify your scraper and pause between requests.

knowledge_points.title: An API beats scraping
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Need: today's weather -> use the weather API (stable JSON, allowed)
Need: prices on a shop with no API -> scraping may be the only way
Scrapers break whenever the page layout changes.
knowledge_points.practice: For described tasks choose API, scraping or neither; predict what breaks a scraper.

knowledge_points.title: Check robots.txt
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser
rp = RobotFileParser()
rp.parse(["User-agent: *", "Disallow: /checkout/"])
print(rp.can_fetch("MyBot", "https://shop.example.com/products/42"))  # True
print(rp.can_fetch("MyBot", "https://shop.example.com/checkout/cart"))  # False
Live code calls rp.set_url(".../robots.txt") and rp.read() instead of parse.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict can_fetch for given rules and URLs.

knowledge_points.title: Say who you are with a User-Agent header
knowledge_points.practice: Add the header to a request; choose an honest User-Agent.

knowledge_points.title: Pause between requests
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import time
for page in range(1, 4):
    r = requests.get(f"{base}?page={page}", timeout=10)
    time.sleep(2)
Without the pause a scraper can hammer a small site; robots.txt may give a Crawl-delay.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a scraper loop with no delay; compute the total wait for n pages.

topics.title: Scraping a page into records and a CSV file
topics.summary: Scrape repeated blocks on a page (cards, rows) into a list of dicts, walk through numbered pages, and save the result as CSV.

knowledge_points.title: One dict per repeated block
knowledge_points.practice: Write the loop for a given page; predict the records it builds.

knowledge_points.title: Why not zip two separate lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
titles = soup.select("h3")
years = soup.select(".year")
If one card has no year, zip(titles, years) pairs every later title with the wrong year.
Looping over cards keeps each title with its own year.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the mismatched pairs for a page with a missing field; choose the safe loop.

knowledge_points.title: Walk through numbered pages
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for page in range(1, 4):

topics.summary: Keep unattended scripts running: retry flaky calls with growing waits, skip one bad item without stopping, log what happened, and limit how much a run does.

knowledge_points.title: Retry with growing waits
knowledge_points.practice: Trace attempts and waits for given failures; compute total wait time.

knowledge_points.title: One bad item should not stop the run
knowledge_points.practice: Move the try so one failure skips one item; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Log what happened
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def log(message, now):
    with open("bot.log", "a") as f:
        f.write(f"{now:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} {message}\n")
# bot.log gets: 2024-10-12 09:00 price checked: 98.5
Nobody watches a scheduled script, so the log is how you find out what it did.
knowledge_points.practice: Write log lines for events; predict the log after a run.

knowledge_points.title: Limit and pace each run
knowledge_points.worked_example:
MAX_ACTIONS = 20
done = 0
for job in jobs:
    if done == MAX_ACTIONS:
        break
    apply(job)
    done += 1
    time.sleep(3)
Caps and pauses keep a bug from sending 1000 emails or getting your account blocked.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many actions run for given lists; add a cap to a loop.

topics.title: Controlling the mouse and keyboard with PyAutoGUI
topics.summary: Move and click the mouse, type and press keys from Python, read a pixel's colour to react to the screen, and keep a stop switch.

knowledge_points.title: Screen coordinates
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import pyautogui   # python3 -m pip install pyautogui
print(pyautogui.size())      # e.g. Size(width=1920, height=1080)
print(pyautogui.position())  # e.g. Point(x=640, y=410)
(0, 0) is the top-left corner; y grows downwards.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict coordinates of screen corners and the centre for given sizes.

knowledge_points.title: Move, click, type, press
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pyautogui.moveTo(500, 300, duration=0.5)
pyautogui.click()
pyautogui.write("hello", interval=0.1)
pyautogui.press("enter")
knowledge_points.practice: Order the actions for a described task; fill in the call for a key press.

knowledge_points.title: Stop switches: FAILSAFE and PAUSE
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pyautogui.FAILSAFE = True   # default: slam the mouse into a corner to stop
pyautogui.PAUSE = 0.2       # wait after every call
Moving to a corner raises pyautogui.FailSafeException and ends the script.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose settings for a safe bot; predict what happens when the mouse hits a corner.

knowledge_points.title: React to the screen
knowledge_points.worked_example:
while True:
    r, g, b = pyautogui.pixel(300, 400)
    if (r, g, b) == (83, 83, 83):   # dark grey cactus pixel
        pyautogui.press("space")
The dinosaur-game bot jumps when an obstacle's colour appears at a fixed point.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the loop for a sequence of pixel colours; fill in the condition.

topics.title: Running code at set times from Python
topics.summary: Repeat a job with a sleep loop, work out how long to wait until the next run with datetime, and run a job only on certain days.

knowledge_points.title: Every N seconds with sleep
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import time
while True:
    check_price()
    time.sleep(60 * 60)   # one hour
The script must keep running; if the computer sleeps or the program crashes, nothing runs.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute sleep values for described intervals; predict how many runs happen in a day.

knowledge_points.title: Seconds until the next run
knowledge_points.worked_example:
now = datetime(2024, 10, 12, 14, 30)
run_at = now.replace(hour=9, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
if run_at <= now:
    run_at += timedelta(days=1)
print(run_at)                         # 2024-10-13 09:00:00
print((run_at - now).total_seconds())  # 66600.0
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the next run time for given 'now' values; fix the missing next-day step.

knowledge_points.title: Only on certain days
knowledge_points.worked_example:
today = date(2024, 10, 14)
if today.weekday() == 0:
    print("Send Monday quote")
# Send Monday quote  (weekday() is 0 for Monday)
knowledge_points.practice: Write day checks (weekdays, first of the month); predict output for given dates.

knowledge_points.title: Run-forever or run-once?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Run-forever: while True + sleep; needs a machine that stays on.
Run-once: do the job and exit; a scheduler (cron, a cloud task) starts it each time.
Run-once scripts are simpler to restart, log and test.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the style for described jobs; convert a run-forever script to run-once.

topics.title: Scheduling scripts with cron and cloud schedulers
topics.summary: Read and write cron schedules, set up a scheduled task in the cloud, and make a script safe to run unattended (absolute paths, environment variables, logs).

knowledge_points.title: Reading a cron schedule
knowledge_points.worked_example:
minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week
0 9 * * 1      -> 09:00 every Monday
*/15 * * * *   -> every 15 minutes
30 7 1 * *     -> 07:30 on the 1st of each month
knowledge_points.practice: Translate cron lines to words and words to cron lines.

knowledge_points.title: A crontab line uses full paths
knowledge_points.worked_example:
0 9 * * * /home/ana/venv/bin/python /home/ana/bots/birthday.py >> /home/ana/bots/cron.log 2>&1
cron does not start in your folder or your venv, so name both in full and keep the output.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix crontab lines that use relative paths or the wrong Python.

knowledge_points.title: Cloud schedulers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
PythonAnywhere: upload the files, Tasks tab, command python3 birthday.py, time in UTC.
The computer that runs it is always on; yours can be off.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert local times to UTC for a schedule; order the setup steps.

knowledge_points.title: Files next to the script, secrets in the environment
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from pathlib import Path
HERE = Path(__file__).parent
rows = (HERE / "birthdays.csv").read_text()
password = os.environ["EMAIL_APP_PASSWORD"]
A scheduler may start the script from another folder; paths built from __file__ still work.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a scheduled script that cannot find its data file; choose what goes in environment variables.
